pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 7-9 (Lower KS2/Grades 2-4): not all minibeasts are insects — applying the six-legs/three-parts rule to sort insects from other groups: spiders (8 legs, 2 parts — arachnids), woodlice (14 legs — crustaceans), worms (no legs), snails (shell + one foot). The 'is it an insect?' sorting game.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 Y4 'Living things and their habitats' — recognise that living things can be grouped in a variety of ways based on observable features.
• Standards — US (NGSS): supports 3-LS4 diversity and classification reasoning; grouping by observable features.
• Operational details — this is APPLYING the body-plan rule as a classification criterion. The key move is reasoning FROM a feature ('8 legs, so not an insect — it's a spider') rather than by appearance or 'creepiness'. Confront the sticky spider-is-an-insect error head-on. Use mixed real sets so children must count and check, not guess.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7): sorts a set into 'insect'/'not insect' using the six-legs rule. Tier B (age 8): explains why a spider is not an insect (8 legs, 2 body parts). Tier C (age 9): names a distinguishing feature for another group (woodlice 14 legs; worms no legs) and justifies each placement by feature.
bestPractices: Anchor sorting to a checkable criterion (count legs, count body parts) rather than appearance or how 'creepy' a creature looks.
Confront the spider-is-an-insect misconception directly and early, with counting as the corrective.
Use mixed real photo sets so children must actually observe and count, not recall a memorised list.
Introduce the other group names (arachnid, crustacean) lightly, tied to their distinguishing feature.
Model the reasoning sentence: 'It has 8 legs and 2 body parts, so it is NOT an insect — it's a spider.'
keyRepresentations: A two-bin (insect / not insect) sorting board, escalating to four bins (insect/arachnid/crustacean/other).
A magnifier/leg-counter tool for checking before deciding.
A side-by-side comparison plate (insect vs spider vs woodlouse vs worm) with counts.
commonMisconceptions: 'Spiders are insects' — the dominant error; spiders have 8 legs and 2 body parts (arachnids).
'Anything small and crawly is an insect' — treating 'insect' as a synonym for bug/minibeast.
'Worms and snails are insects' — they lack the six-legs/three-parts plan entirely.
'Woodlice are insects' — they are crustaceans with 14 legs.
Sorting by size, colour or scariness instead of by counted features.

learn.summary: For ages 7-9 (Lower KS2/Grades 2-4), learners apply a checkable body-plan rule — an adult insect has 6 legs and 3 body parts — to sort minibeasts into 'insect' and 'not insect', then into finer groups (arachnid, crustacean, other). The core move is reasoning FROM a counted feature ('8 legs and 2 body parts, so it's an arachnid like a spider — not an insect') rather than by appearance, size, or how 'creepy' a creature looks. The activity confronts the dominant 'spiders/worms/woodlice are all insects' misconception head-on, using counting as the corrective.

activities.title: Is it an insect? Sort-and-count
feedback: If a learner drops the spider into INSECT, have them re-count its legs one at a time: marking or lighting legs 1 through 8 and splitting the body into 2 parts shows 'arachnid, not an insect'.
When a sort is justified by 'it's small' or 'it lives in the garden', redirect: 'Two things can both be small — only the leg count and body parts decide. What did you count?'
If a learner insists a spider has 6 legs to make it fit, count the legs together by touching each one; separate 'what I want it to be' from 'what I actually counted' — 8 legs means not an insect.
Confirm correct feature-based reasoning: '6 legs and 3 parts, so insect — yes, that's exactly how classification works.'
activities.rationale: Anchoring the sort to a checkable criterion (count legs, count body parts) and making the learner count BEFORE deciding turns any correction into one driven by the learner's own observation. Confronting the spider misconception early with counting as the corrective targets the most sticky, over-broad 'any small crawly thing is an insect' error. Mixed real photo sets require observation rather than recall of a memorised list.
sourceClaims: KS2 Y4 requires pupils to recognise that living things can be grouped in a variety of ways based on observable features.
Insects (6 legs, 3 body parts) are distinguished from arachnids (8 legs, 2 body parts), crustaceans (e.g. woodlice, many legs), and other invertebrate groups by observable features.
learnerActions: Take a mixed set of real minibeast photos (e.g. ant, beetle, spider, woodlouse, worm, snail) and two bins labelled INSECT and NOT AN INSECT.
Before placing each creature, count its legs and its body parts — touching or marking each leg as you count so you don't miss any.
Place the creature in a bin and say the reason aloud in the form: 'It has ___ legs and ___ body parts, so it is / is not an insect.'
Check the spider carefully: count all 8 legs and notice its body is in 2 parts; place it in NOT AN INSECT and name it an arachnid.

Check the woodlouse (14 legs) and the worm (no legs) the same way. Handle the snail as a clear non-insect 'other': it has no legs (a shell and one muscular foot), so it fails the six-legs test — do not try to fit it to a leg-count group. Confirm the beetle and ant have 6 legs and 3 parts and belong in INSECT.
Expert round: re-sort into four bins — insect / arachnid / crustacean / other — and justify each placement by its distinguishing feature.
activities.intendedInsight: Classification means grouping by a definite, countable feature, not by appearance. An insect is defined by 6 legs and 3 body parts; creatures that fail this test (spider 8 legs/2 parts, woodlouse 14 legs, worm no legs, snail no legs/shell+foot) belong to other groups.

activities.title: Comparison plate: features side by side
feedback: If a learner cannot name a distinguishing feature, point them back to the revealed counts and ask which number is different from the insect's six.
Reinforce the group names lightly and always tied to the feature: 'arachnid — the 8-legged one'.
activities.rationale: A comparison plate teaches the distinguishing features clearly and supports introducing group names (arachnid, crustacean) tied to their feature. Its narrow limit as a scaffold: a static comparison shows the features but does not itself exercise the sort-and-check reasoning, so pair it with the sorting activity.
sourceClaims: Insects (6 legs, 3 body parts) are distinguished from arachnids (8 legs, 2 body parts), crustaceans (e.g. woodlice, many legs), and other invertebrate groups by observable features.
learnerActions: Study a side-by-side plate of an insect, a spider, a woodlouse, and a worm.
For each creature, reveal or record its leg count and number of body parts (tap-to-reveal counts work if the plate is interactive).

Fill in a feature-to-group link for the creatures on the plate: 6 legs and 3 body parts → insect, 8 legs and 2 body parts → arachnid, woodlouse with 14 legs → crustacean, no legs → worm/other. (Having many legs does not by itself make an animal a crustacean: centipedes and millipedes have many legs but are not crustaceans.)
State what makes each group different in one sentence.
activities.intendedInsight: Each minibeast group has a distinguishing observable feature; seeing the counts side by side makes the contrasts explicit before sorting new cases.

activities.title: The spider sets the record straight
feedback: If the learner accepts 'spiders are bugs so they're insects', return to the count: 8 legs is the single feature that decides it.

For the caterpillar prompt, clarify that a caterpillar is the larval life stage of an insect (it becomes a butterfly or moth) — being an insect or not is about the group, not how it looks at one stage.
activities.rationale: A playful in-role exchange is a motivating way to surface the dominant misconception, though it surfaces rather than drills the criterion — the sorting activity exercises the reasoning more directly, so use this to open or discuss, not as the main practice.
learnerActions: Act out or read a short exchange in which a spider objects: 'I'm NOT an insect — count my legs!'
Respond by actually counting the spider's legs (8) and body parts (2) and stating the group it belongs to.

Discuss a stage-vs-group counterexample: a caterpillar looks worm-like but is the young stage of an insect that becomes a butterfly or moth. Treat this as a discussion of life stage versus group only — not as a leg-counting case, since a caterpillar's prolegs can make a raw leg count misleading.
Discuss: could something be tiny and live in the garden and STILL not be an insect? Give an example (spider, worm, woodlouse, snail).
activities.intendedInsight: Surfacing the misconception in role makes the learner defend or reject 'insect' with the counted feature rather than with a feeling about what counts as a 'bug'.

activities.title: Explain-your-decision check
feedback: Full grasp: sorts all four correctly, rejects the spider with '8 legs / 2 body parts', and explains differences (worm = no legs, woodlouse = 14) rather than reciting one fact.
Partial grasp: states the six-legs rule but applies it unevenly — e.g. rejects the worm but slips the spider or woodlouse in; prompt them to count again and give the feature reason each time.
Gap: puts spider/worm/woodlouse in the insect box and sorts by size or creepiness — re-establish counting legs as the sole gate before sorting.
activities.rationale: A two-tier check (sort + 'how did you decide?') exposes whether the sort is driven by the counted rule or by the over-broad 'bug = insect' feeling. Asking for the feature reason, not just the category, discriminates genuine understanding. Correct answer: the spider is not an insect (8 legs, 2 parts, an arachnid); only the ant is an insect (6 legs, 3 parts); the woodlouse (14 legs) and worm (no legs) are not.
sourceClaims: KS2 Y4 requires pupils to recognise that living things can be grouped in a variety of ways based on observable features.
learnerActions: Someone put a spider in the 'insect' box — decide whether that is right.
Sort these four — spider, ant, woodlouse, worm — into 'insect' and 'not insect'.
For each one, say HOW you decided (which feature you counted).
Answer the follow-ups: give the one feature that proves the spider is out; say whether a 14-legged woodlouse is an insect and which rule tells you.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to state the deciding feature for each creature distinguishes a learner who owns the six-legs/three-parts rule from one relying on 'it's small and creepy'.

constraints: Sorting must be driven by a checkable criterion (count legs, count body parts), never by size, colour, habitat, or how 'creepy' a creature looks.
Use mixed real photo sets so learners must actually observe and count, not recall a memorised list.
Introduce group names (arachnid, crustacean) lightly and always tied to the distinguishing feature, not as isolated vocabulary.
The comparison plate is a scaffold for learning the features; on its own it shows the features but does not exercise the sort-and-check reasoning, so pair it with active sorting.

Matching a creature to its group can assess recognition of the rule but does not by itself require the learner to count and construct the decision; include at least one task where the learner counts and justifies independently.

The caterpillar example concerns life stage vs taxonomic group — handle as a discussion point only, not as a leg-counting case, keeping the focus on the six-legs/three-parts criterion for the general insect body plan.
The snail (shell + one foot, no legs) is a non-arthropod example; use it as a clear non-insect 'other' case rather than trying to classify it by the leg-count rule.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Both source claims are marked verified:false in the original. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Both legacy sources are marked unverified (DfE curriculum reference and NHM/AES invertebrate group references). Treat the leg/body-part counts (insect 6/3, spider 8/2, woodlouse 14, worm 0) as standard references but confirm against a current authority if used for assessment.

The original 3D-interactive entry claimed '3D adds cost without insight' for this topic; retained only as a scoped observation that countable-feature classification is not inherently spatial — this is a design judgement, not an established pedagogical law, and is not asserted as a universal claim here.

Woodlouse leg count is stated as 14 throughout; adult woodlice typically have 14 legs (7 pairs), consistent with the source — flagged only so a reviewer can confirm against the chosen reference set. Source claim 2 itself only says 'many legs'.

The original framed the correction as 'the moment the rule beats the guess'; the underlying principle (a learner-counted correction is more persuasive) is preserved without claiming any single medium is necessary to achieve it.

A caterpillar is itself an insect (larval stage); it is kept out of any leg-counting task because its true legs plus prolegs can make a raw count misleading, and is used only to discuss life stage versus group.

Independent re-review confirmed the snail handling (zero-legs 'other', not force-fit to the leg-count rule) and the caterpillar handling (butterfly OR moth, discussion-only) are consistently applied across actions, feedback, constraints and notes; no categorical medium-superiority claims remain in learner-facing text.

probeDeeper: 'You said the spider is out. Give me the one feature that proves it.'
'A woodlouse has 14 legs. Insect or not — and which rule tells you?'
'A caterpillar looks like a worm but turns into a butterfly. Is a caterpillar an insect?' (a stage-vs-group counterexample)
'Could something be tiny and live in the garden and STILL not be an insect? Give me an example.'
assess.correctAnswer: The spider is NOT an insect — it has 8 legs and 2 body parts (it's an arachnid). Only the ant is an insect (6 legs, 3 body parts). The woodlouse (14 legs) and the worm (no legs) are also not insects. The deciding rule is the six-legs test: an insect has exactly six legs and three body parts; anything else is 'not insect'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks any small crawling creature is an insect — 'spiders, worms, woodlice are all insects, they're all bugs'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the six-legs rule the sole gate: count legs before sorting. Spider = 8 → out. Let the count overrule the 'it's a bug' feeling.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — spiders are little crawly bugs, so they're insects
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Puts spider/worm/woodlouse in the insect box; justifies by size or creepiness, not leg count

errorPatterns.pattern: Sorts by size or habitat ('it lives in the garden / it's tiny') instead of body features
errorPatterns.nextMove: Redirect to countable features. Two things can both be small; only leg count and body parts decide 'insect'. Practise saying the reason as '6 legs, so insect' / '8 legs, so not'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: reason is 'because it's small' or 'it's in the soil', never legs or body parts

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts a spider as 6 legs (miscounts to force it to fit the insect rule)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the spider's legs together, touching each — 8. Then apply the rule honestly: 8 → not an insect. Separate 'I want it to be' from 'what I counted'.
errorPatterns.distractor: A spider has six legs, so it counts as an insect
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists the spider has 6 legs so it can stay an insect

responseLevels.gap: Puts spider/worm/woodlouse in the insect box; sorts by size or creepiness; no feature-based rule.
responseLevels.full: Sorts all four correctly, rejects the spider with '8 legs / 2 body parts', and applies the six-legs-three-parts rule consistently across new cases — explaining a difference (worm = no legs, woodlouse = 14) rather than reciting one fact.
responseLevels.partial: Sorts most correctly and can state the six-legs rule, but applies it unevenly — e.g. rejects the worm but slips the spider or woodlouse in, or can't consistently give the feature-based reason.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Someone put a spider in the 'insect' box. Is that right? Sort these for me — spider, ant, woodlouse, worm — into 'insect' and 'not insect', and each time tell me HOW you decided.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who owns the rule applies the six-legs/three-parts test consistently and rejects the spider with a reason. A child who thinks 'insect = any small crawly thing' puts spider, woodlouse and worm all in the insect box — the second-tier 'how did you decide?' exposes whether the sort is driven by the rule or by 'it's little and creepy'. This is the classic over-broad 'bug/insect' misconception.
